Conjunctions

In the English language, there are some words that are called “conjunctions”. A conjunction is a word that you can use to connect parts of speech like: other words, phrases or sentences. For, so, whether and or are common conjunctions.
Can you tell us whether we are going to continue with the next topics or not?
Revenue, can be an example of a data warehouse, for it incorporates data from other operational systems that contain information like student tuition data, alumni gift data, financial aid data.
Some of the key features of a data warehouse are that you can use it for reporting and for the analytical processing of data; so, it organizes data in a subject-oriented manner.

For is a preposition, but you can also use it as a conjunction. It has a similar meaning as that of because or since .

Example:
John thinks he is a good programmer, for he studied several years to be one.

So is another word that you can use as a conjunction as well, it has a similar meaning to therefore or consequently .

Example:
Mary won the lottery, so she will be buying lots of things.

Whether and or are two conjunctions that people commonly use together or in the same sentence, and they express a doubt or choice between two possibilities.

Example:
I want you to tell me whether to use data warehouse or operational databases.
Zero Conditional Starting With the Main Cause in Negative

The zero conditional is one of the four types of conditionals we have in English. You use it to talk about a real situation (condition) and the result of that situation (result). This conditional has two parts; the if clause and the main clause or result .
You don't have to use a data warehouse if you don't want to. That's why you have operational databases.
We can use the zero conditional starting with the main clause or the result in negative. Remember we need to use the present simple here, so the structure would go like this:

images.text:
Student: Hello, teacher! Can you tell us whether we are going to continue with the next topics or not?
Teacher: You cannot continue with the contents of the program if you don't know about data warehouses and operational databases, so today we will talk about them.
Student: Okay, proceed.

Teacher: Well, for starters, a data warehouse is where an organization or company keeps information electrically. Some of the key features of a data warehouse are that you can use it for reporting and for the analytical processing of data; so, it organizes data in a subject-oriented manner. Revenue can be an example of a data warehouse, for it incorporates data from other operational systems that contain information like student tuition data, alumni gift data, financial aid data.
Student: And operational databases?
Teacher: Alright, you don't have to use a data warehouse if you don't want to. That's why you have operational databases. An operational database is the one that allows users to access it and update it on a regular basis, its key features are that it has to deal with the transaction processing of the business. The approach that operational databases use is OLTP which means On Line Transaction Processing Databases. Let me give you an example. If a company wants to track stock and see how many items of something they have available, they use an operational database because they can see all that information in real time.

Student: You should tell us whether there are more similarities or differences between these two concepts.
Teacher: Absolutely! Let me give you a brief comparison of the two. They are similar, for both of them are databases and you can use them for the same purpose: storage and organization of data. Now, some differences are that data warehouses have historical data which facilitates analysis, but operational databases only have current data, so they only concentrate on the data being recorded as of now. Another difference is that you don't have the opportunity to change or delete data if you use data warehouses, but with operational databases, you can modify or even delete data.
